chunks: Bypass, decoupling and bulk capacitors. The question: What is a bypass/decoupling capacitor? What about a bulk capacitor? What is the difference?
A decoupling (or bypass) capacitor is a small capacitor placed right at a chip's power pin.
It supplies the quick bursts of current the chip needs and sends high-frequency noise to ground. A bulk capacitor is a much bigger one near where power enters.
It supports slower, larger changes in demand. You usually need both, because each works best in a different range of speeds.
Imagine you are working at a desk. A glass of water on the desk is instantly available but small. That is the decoupling capacitor.
A water cooler down the hall holds much more but takes a moment to reach. That is the bulk capacitor. The town water supply is the regulator. It has plenty but responds slowly.
The analogy ignores noise, which the small capacitor also filters out.
Each stage supplies the current the previous one can't deliver fast enough. The stages overlap in frequency; the chain is limited by the weakest link, usually inductance.
Decoupling / bypass capacitor: a small capacitor at a chip's (IC's) supply pin that handles fast current bursts and noise.
Bulk capacitor: a large capacitor, tens to hundreds of µF, for slower changes in demand. Regulator: the circuit that makes the supply voltage.
It is slow to react to fast load steps. Transient current: a sudden change in the current a chip draws.
Target impedance: the highest supply impedance you can allow: the allowed voltage dip divided by the current step.
A chip suddenly draws an extra 1 amps for 1 microseconds before the regulator can react. You allow the supply rail to dip by 100 millivolts.
The capacitor must supply that charge: C at least I change in t over change in V equals 1 times 10 to the -6 over 0. 1 equals 10 microfarads.
A small 100 nanofarads part cannot do this alone, so a bigger one covers the gap. That is the whole idea.
"A decoupling or bypass cap is a small ceramic, about 100 nanofarads, right at the IC's supply pin.
It supplies the fast current bursts the chip needs and shunts high-frequency noise to ground.
A bulk capacitor is large, tens to hundreds of microfarads, near the power entry or load, holding the rail up through slower load steps while the regulator reacts.
The difference is the frequency band: big caps have high ESL so they only work at low frequency, small ones work to tens of MHz, so you use both, smallest closest to the pin."
